common_name: Superbells Doublette Love Swept Calibrachoa (Double-Flowered Deep Pink Million Bells Edged in White)
scientific_name: Calibrachoa x hybrida 'Superbells Doublette Love Swept'

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Doublette Love Swept opens the Doublette line, a newer Proven Winners double-flower series distinct from the older Superbells Double selections already in this dataset.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer to prevent the iron chlorosis calibrachoa is prone to in alkaline media. Doublette Love Swept carries small, fully double blooms that read like miniature roses, deep pink at the center and edged in a fine rim of white, on a mounding-trailing plant that cascades up to 16 inches over a container rim. Unlike single-flowered calibrachoa the extra petal layers add some weight to each bloom, so keep the mix evenly moist rather than letting it dry to wilting, and give the plant a mid-summer trim to refresh branching if the crown thins. Flowers are self-cleaning and need no deadheading, blooming continuously from planting until hard frost.
sources: Proven Winners — Superbells Doublette series cultivar notes

common_name: Superbells Holy Cow Calibrachoa (Yellow Million Bells Blushed with Pink)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Holy Cow is one of a trio of exclamatory Superbells names alongside Holy Moly, already in this dataset, and Holy Smokes.

directions: Grow in full sun to part sun in well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to keep the foliage from yellowing with iron chlorosis. Holy Cow carries a soft yellow base blushed and streaked with pink, a softer bicolor than the sharper yellow-and-cherry mottling of Superbells Holy Moly already grown here, on a mounding-trailing plant that cascades up to 24 inches. The tiny petunia-like flowers are self-cleaning and require no deadheading, blooming continuously from planting to hard frost. It tolerates heat well once established and benefits from a light mid-season trim to keep the mound dense rather than sparse.

common_name: Superbells Holy Smokes Calibrachoa (Yellow Million Bells Splashed with Blue-Purple)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Holy Smokes rounds out the exclamatory Superbells trio with Holy Cow and Holy Moly, already in this dataset.

directions: Plant in full sun to part sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix and feed regularly with an acid-forming, iron-rich fertilizer, since calibrachoa yellows quickly in high-pH media. Holy Smokes is unusual for the genus in pairing a soft yellow base with irregular splashes of blue-purple rather than the pink or red tones typical of most bicolor Superbells, giving it a smoky, painterly look distinct from any other calibrachoa already in this dataset. It builds a mounding, trailing plant that cascades up to 24 inches over a basket or pot rim, self-cleaning without any deadheading and flowering continuously from planting through hard frost. It holds its color well through summer heat with consistent moisture and weekly feeding.

common_name: Superbells Tropical Sunrise Calibrachoa (Bicolor Pink, Coral, and Yellow Million Bells)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; a Proven Winners top-selling selection prized for its sunrise-toned streaked blooms.

directions: Grow in full sun to part sun in well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, and feed weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to prevent the iron chlorosis calibrachoa develops in alkaline soil. Tropical Sunrise produces variable streaks of yellow and pinkish-red on each bloom, blending pink, coral, and yellow tones on the same flower for a sunset-like effect that distinguishes it from the solid or evenly split bicolor patterns of Superbells Lemon Slice and Coralina already grown here. It mounds and trails up to 18 inches, making a strong spiller for hanging baskets and window boxes, and self-cleans without deadheading, blooming from planting to hard frost. It is notably heat tolerant and rewards regular feeding with dense, uninterrupted color through summer.

common_name: Superbells Miss Lilac Calibrachoa (Lavender Million Bells with Yellow Eye)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Miss Lilac fills a soft lavender niche between the deeper violet-blue of Superbells Blue and the pink tones of Callie Rose, both already in this dataset.

directions: Plant in full sun to part sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to keep foliage green and prevent iron chlorosis. Miss Lilac produces soft lavender-purple blooms centered with a sunny yellow eye, a gentler pastel shade distinct from the saturated violet-blue of Superbells Blue already grown here. Its mounding, trailing habit cascades up to 30 inches, among the longest reaches in the Superbells line, making it a strong spiller for large hanging baskets. The self-cleaning flowers need no deadheading and bloom continuously from planting to hard frost, holding their color well through summer heat with consistent moisture.

common_name: Superbells Watermelon Punch Calibrachoa (Coral-Pink Million Bells with Red-and-Black Eye)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Watermelon Punch belongs to the vigorous, heat-tolerant Punch subseries of Superbells alongside Pomegranate Punch and Coralberry Punch, both already in this dataset.

directions: Grow in full sun to part sun in well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to prevent the iron chlorosis common to calibrachoa in high-pH media. Watermelon Punch carries rich coral-pink petals centered with a dark red-and-black eye, a warmer, more saturated tone than the deep velvet red of Superbells Pomegranate Punch already grown here. As a Punch subseries member it is bred for extra vigor and heat tolerance, mounding and trailing up to 30 inches, and it earned multiple university trial awards in 2019 for garden performance. Flowers self-clean without deadheading, blooming from planting to hard frost, and a mid-summer trim keeps growth dense and floriferous rather than leggy.

directions: Plant in full sun to part sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix, and feed weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to keep foliage green and avoid the iron chlorosis common in calibrachoa grown in alkaline soil. Honeyberry blends soft pink and honey-yellow tones across each small petunia-like bloom, a muted pastel combination distinct from the brighter bicolor patterns of Superbells Lemon Slice and Tropical Sunrise already grown here. Its mounding, trailing habit cascades up to 30 inches, well suited to large hanging baskets and elevated containers. The self-cleaning flowers need no deadheading and bloom continuously from planting to hard frost, tolerating summer heat well with consistent watering.

common_name: Million Bells Trailing Blue Calibrachoa (Suntory-Bred Trailing Blue-Purple Million Bells)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Million Bells is Suntory's original trademarked calibrachoa line, sold alongside but distinct from the Proven Winners Superbells and Syngenta Callie selections already in this dataset.

directions: Grow in full sun to part sun in well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to prevent iron deficiency chlorosis. Trailing Blue is part of Suntory's Million Bells line, the breeding program that gave the genus its common name and a distinct commercial series from the Proven Winners Superbells and Syngenta Callie selections already represented in this dataset; it produces a profusion of cascading blue-purple flowers on a lower, flatter plant than most Superbells selections, with trailing stems reaching 20 to 30 inches. The tiny petunia-like blooms are self-cleaning and need no deadheading, flowering continuously from planting to hard frost. It performs best in hanging baskets and window boxes where its long trailing stems can spill freely.

common_name: Superbells Magic Double Grapefruit Calibrachoa (Double-Flowered Million Bells That Shifts from Yellow to Pink)
scientific_name: Calibrachoa x hybrida 'Superbells Magic Double Grapefruit'

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Magic Double Grapefruit builds on the single-flowered Pink Lemonade selection with fully double blooms and the same temperature-driven color shift.

directions: Plant in full sun to part sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix, feeding weekly with an acid-forming fertilizer to prevent iron chlorosis. Magic Double Grapefruit is genuinely unusual among calibrachoa for its temperature-driven color shift: individual double blooms open lemon yellow and take on soft pink tones as they age in summer heat, so a single plant can carry yellow, pink, and blended grapefruit-toned flowers all at once, distinguishing it from every other double-flowered Superbells selection already in this dataset. It mounds and trails in typical Superbells fashion, self-cleaning without deadheading and blooming continuously from planting to hard frost. Consistent moisture and regular feeding keep the doubled flowers full-sized and the color transition vivid through the season.
sources: Proven Winners — Superbells Magic series notes
